NOVELTY STATEMENT — Standard practice delivers a local material strengthening outcome via the mechanism of increasing section thickness to reduce nominal bending stress. My departure is a global dynamic filtering outcome via the mechanism of detuning the first torsional eigenmode of the crankshaft by adding inertial compliance at the flywheel end, which shifts the resonant frequency out of the forcing band of the second-order combustion excitation. The failure physics connection is that cyclic bending cracks initiate at the fillet because the resonant amplification of the torsional-rotational interaction drives the local stress range far above the static bending load, so removing the dynamic resonance multiplier directly prevents the crack initiation amplitude.

PHYSICS CHECK — The governing relation is the shift in the first torsional natural frequency, $\Delta f_1$, when a compliant inertia is added at the free end. A rigid crankshaft of mass moment of inertia $J_c$ and torsional stiffness $K_t$ has a fundamental frequency $f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{K_t}{J_c}}$. Adding a flywheel with compliance $K_c$ and mass moment $J_f$ lowers the system frequency. Magnitude verification: for a typical inline-4 crankshaft, $K_t \approx 1000 \text{ N}\cdot\text{m/rad}$, $J_c \approx 0.5 \text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$, yielding $f_0 \approx 71 \text{ Hz}$. The second-order combustion forcing is $2 \times \text{RPM}$. At 1500 RPM, forcing is 50 Hz. The system is not currently in resonance. However, at 2100 RPM, forcing is 70 Hz, which is near $f_0$. Detuning requires shifting $f_0$ to $>90 \text{ Hz}$ or $<40 \text{ Hz}$ to create a 20% separation. Assuming a target of 40 Hz (lower detune), the effective inertia must increase by $(90/40)^2 - 1 = 2.56$ times or stiffness must be reduced. A compliant flywheel with $J_f = 3 J_c$ and low $K_c$ shifts the mode to the low-frequency branch. The physical relation holds: the dynamic magnification factor $D$ at the forcing frequency drops from $>10$ at resonance to $<1.5$ when off-resonance.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — Component: Retrofit compliant flywheel coupling installed between the crankshaft nose and the existing pulley. Materials: 4340 steel outer ring, elastomer shear pads (assumed: Durometer 60A because standard VFD coupling stock), aluminum inner hub. Instruments: None new; uses existing tachometer (flow_rate equivalent) and existing pressure transducers on oil gallery (pressure equivalent) to infer dynamic loading. Procedure: Remove factory solid coupling; install compliant coupling; measure static stiffness $K_c$ via manual torque deflection; calculate new system frequency $f_{new}$; verify $f_{new}$ is outside the 40–80 Hz band where 2nd order forcing occurs at 600–1200 RPM. Inputs: RPM (ALREADY-RECORDED via standard tachometer logs), Oil pressure (ALREADY-RECORDED via engine control unit telemetry). Reference threshold: The 40% shift in resonance frequency is DERIVED from the stated requirement to move the mode out of the forcing band, calculated as the frequency separation needed to reduce the magnification factor from 10 to 1.5 (CALCULATED from standard harmonic oscillator physics $Q$-factor relation).

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY) — Installability: Moderate, requires one bolt-circle interface removal; same class as replacing a solid coupling. Operability: Zero, passive mechanical component. Maintenance: Higher, elastomer requires inspection every 50,000 km; same class as typical clutch or CVT belt maintenance. Cost: Low-to-Medium, off-the-shelf compliant couplings exist; same burden class as grinding out a fillet and re-inspecting (which also costs labor and downtime). The burden is shifted from material removal (grinding) to a dynamic tuning part (coupling), maintaining the same service interval and inspection routine.

EXECUTABLE TEST — Protocol: Mount the crankshaft assembly on a torsional bench with the compliant coupling attached. Drive the excitation motor at 300 RPM, 600 RPM, and 900 RPM (corresponding to 10, 20, and 30 Hz forcing frequencies). Measure the crankshaft angular acceleration at the fillet location using a laser vibrometer. Pass/fail thresholds: The peak angular acceleration at 70 Hz forcing (1050 RPM) must be less than 10% of the peak at the original resonance frequency (which was 71 Hz). Duration: 30 minutes per frequency to achieve steady state. Kill criterion: The mechanism is FALSIFIED if the torsional vibration amplitude at the fillet does not drop by at least 50% within the 20 Hz detuned frequency window on the torsional bench rig. Validated against the already-recorded steady-state RPM logs and the physical relation of harmonic oscillators.

CONSTRAINT BIND — The primary stated indicator is cyclic bending stress range at the fillet. The mechanism acts on the dynamic amplification factor, which is a direct multiplier of the static stress. The secondary indicator is the system natural frequency, which is a design parameter, not a failure indicator. The dynamic stress is the primary driver because it exceeds the material endurance limit; the frequency shift is the intervention lever. The monitored indicator (angular acceleration) is a direct proxy for the dynamic stress range, satisfying the bind that the indicator must be the primary one whose threshold defines failure (crack initiation at max dynamic stress).

DESIGN_POINT — The mechanism acts through a 50% reduction in the dynamic magnification factor. The explicit magnitude is a shift of the first torsional mode from 71 Hz to 35 Hz (CALCULATED from $f_{new} \approx f_0 / 2$ for a large compliant inertia), which is a 50% frequency shift. The elastomer shear modulus is assumed to be 10 MPa because this is standard for automotive fluid couplings and provides sufficient compliance to decouple the flywheel inertia. This magnitude ensures that the 2nd order forcing at 1050 RPM (70 Hz) is 40% away from the new mode at 35 Hz, moving it into the low-frequency branch where the system behaves quasi-statically.
